title: The king who stayed king
hookLine: a king hears the sage Yajnavalkya say the knower's body lies like a snake's old skin. then he goes on ruling
carry: jivanmukti: free while still living in the body

lines: A THOUSAND COWS: TEACH ME MORE.
cards: King Janaka of Videha loves hard questions, and his court is well-known for them.

When the sage Yajnavalkya visits, the king keeps him talking, about dreams, about deep sleep, about what happens at death, and again and again he says: I'll give you a thousand cows, sir; teach me more, for freedom.
So Yajnavalkya describes the one who has let go of every desire in the heart. Such a person, he says, reaches Brahman here, in this life. And he gives a picture.
As a snake's cast-off skin lies on an anthill, dead and thrown away, so lies this body. The shape is still there; the snake has moved on. Janaka didn't leave his throne.

teach.h: A WISH, A POINTER, A SOURCE, A HARMONY.
teach.b: Shankara reaches for this skin near the end of his comment on the Brahma Sutra's fourth line, the last of the four lines we've followed this week. One, the wish to know Brahman. Two, that from which this world comes.
Three, the source of scripture. Four, the texts all connect in it. Then the image.
Being embodied, Shankara says, comes from the old mix-up, the I taken for the body. When knowing removes the mix-up, the body doesn't vanish. It goes on walking, eating, getting tired.

teach.h: THE BODY NO LONGER TAKEN FOR THE SELF.
teach.b: But it's no longer taken for the self. Like the skin on the anthill, it keeps its shape, and nobody is trapped inside it.
Advaita teachers call this jivanmukti, freedom while still living.
And Shankara adds a test that's hard to forget: someone who has truly understood doesn't live in the turning world the way they did before; someone who still does hasn't understood yet.

Many seekers renounce everything, as Shankara himself did; for many Hindus, Janaka shows the knowing doesn't need a cave. Today we're told to find ourselves in our roles: the job, the grades, the image.
This teaching says you can carry every role and be held by none.

how: Advaita Vedanta teachers often read the Brahma Sutra's first four lines with students as a summary of the whole work, and hold up sages like King Janaka as pictures of freedom while still living.

o: a theory about the body, learned by heart
a practice of leaving the body behind
knowing that changes where you stand

games.q: the king and the skin — tap the pairs.
p: the body, no longer taken for the self

s: for Shankara, the body vanishes when someone comes to know
it goes on, like the skin on the anthill, but it's no longer taken for the self.
the Gita names Janaka among those who reached perfection through action
Hindus remember him as a king who knew the self and kept ruling.
Shankara says someone can understand and live exactly as before
he says whoever still lives in the turning world as before hasn't understood yet.

games.q: you've read the four opening lines with Shankara. someone asks: so has the knower left their body behind? what does he answer?
o: the body goes on, but it isn't taken for the self.
games.why: like a snake's cast-off skin: the shape remains, and nobody is trapped inside it.

practice: Feel the whole body sitting, from the soles of the feet to the top of the head, and let the chair or the floor carry its weight. Then name, quietly, the roles you'll carry today: student, child, friend, worker.
Hold each one lightly, like a skin with nobody trapped inside. If you pray, offer the day's roles; if you don't, simply rest.

wordCard.voice: Jnana. Knowing. For Shankara, the knowing that removes the mix-up and changes where you stand, as a snake leaves its skin behind.

orig.note: Sanskrit: freedom while living; Advaita's word for the knower whose body goes on.

carryVoice: Your line: jivanmukti: free while still living in the body. Janaka kept his throne. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3–4.4 (Yajnavalkya teaches King Janaka of Videha; Janaka's repeated 'I give you a thousand cows, sir; teach me further, for freedom')

Shankara, Brahma Sutra Bhashya 1.1.4, closing section (embodiment rooted in false knowledge; the knower bodiless even while living; one who has understood does not belong to the round of rebirth as before)

Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.7 (when all desires in the heart are let go, the mortal becomes immortal and reaches Brahman here; as the slough of a snake lies on an anthill, dead and cast away, so lies this body)
Bhagavad Gita 3.20 (Janaka and others reached perfection through action)
